props.subtitle: Teach people to use IT systems and software in a safe copy, when they can't touch the real thing
props.title: Interactive User Manuals

bullets: Why simulate: least privilege, production data, irreversible actions and licence cost
Five approaches, from screenshot guides to hotspot simulations, DOM capture, UI clones and training sandboxes, and their tools
Maintainability: upkeep cost, drift detection, version labels, and what can be done as code or with AI
Creation principles: task-first, selective fidelity, safe to fail, and Watch → Try → Test
what.definition: An interactive user manual is a simulation of a software system that lets people practise real tasks (clicking, typing, making mistakes) without using the live system.
what.summary: Trainees often aren't allowed to touch the real software: they lack the role, it holds real people's data, or one wrong click sends real money. This topic covers why we simulate, the five ways to build a simulation and the tools for each, how to keep it matching the real software release after release (including as code and with AI), and the principles that make a simulation actually teach.

why.impact: Teams that pick an approach without thinking about upkeep end up with the Drifted Phantom UI: a simulation of screens that no longer exist, which trains people to do the wrong thing with confidence.
why.summary: A manual people can practise in beats a manual people read, but only while it still matches the real software.

categories.analogy: A flight simulator: trainee pilots practise engine failures long before anyone hands them the keys to a real aircraft.
categories.description: Least-privilege access control means trainees often have no account or role that allows the actions they must learn.
categories.details: Good security gives each person only the permissions their current job needs. A new hire in the finance team may not get the 'approve payment' role until after training, and an IT trainee should never hold domain-admin rights just to practise. So the very actions the manual must teach are the ones the learner is not allowed to perform. A simulation lets them rehearse the approver's screens without ever holding the approver's role.
inScope: Roles granted only after training or certification
Admin and approver screens that trainees must not reach
Separation-of-duties rules (one person cannot both request and approve)
outOfScope: Protecting the data inside the system (see Production Data)
categories.primaryFocus: Teaching actions the learner is not yet authorised to perform
categories.subtitle: No role, no practice
categories.title: Least-Privilege Access

categories.analogy: Medical students practise on mannequins, not on the patient in bed 12.
categories.description: Real systems hold production data (customer PII, patient or financial records) that trainees must not see or change.
categories.details: A hospital system shows real patients, a CRM shows real customers, and a banking back office shows real balances. Letting trainees browse that data for practice breaks privacy law (such as GDPR or Thailand's PDPA) and the organisation's own policies. Even a read-only training account still exposes personal data to people who have no business need to see it.
inScope: Personally identifiable information (PII)
Patient, financial and HR records
Privacy and data-protection obligations
outOfScope: Actions that change the world outside the system (see Irreversible Actions)
categories.primaryFocus: Keeping personal and confidential records away from practice
categories.subtitle: Real people's records are not a practice ground
categories.title: Production Data

categories.analogy: Fire drills use a pretend fire so people can practise the exit route without anyone getting burned.
categories.description: Some actions are irreversible or high-impact in a live system, such as issuing a refund, deleting a record or changing a network rule.
categories.details: A refund sends real money, a deleted record may be gone for good, an e-mail blast reaches real customers, and a wrong firewall rule can cut off a whole office. Learning by trial and error is how people learn software best, but in a live system every error is a real incident. A simulation removes the consequence while keeping the practice.
inScope: Money movement: refunds, payments, payroll
Destructive actions: delete, purge, overwrite
Outbound effects: e-mails, orders, network and security changes
outOfScope: Whether the learner is allowed to act at all (see Least-Privilege Access)
categories.primaryFocus: Letting learners make mistakes that cost nothing
categories.subtitle: Some buttons cannot be un-pressed
categories.title: Irreversible Actions

categories.analogy: A driving school doesn't buy every student a car; it shares a few dual-control cars and uses a simulator for the rest.
categories.description: Per-seat licences and shared environments make it costly to give every trainee a real system to practise on.
categories.details: Enterprise software such as ERP, CRM or ITSM platforms is usually licensed per user, and extra non-production environments cost more again. A class of 200 new staff each needing a seat just to practise for a week is hard to justify. Shared test environments are also busy with developers and testers, who do not want trainees changing their data.
inScope: Per-user licensing of enterprise platforms
Cost and upkeep of extra non-production environments
Shared test environments that trainees would disrupt
outOfScope: The cost of building and maintaining the simulation itself (see Keeping It Alive)
categories.primaryFocus: Scaling practice without scaling licences
categories.subtitle: A real seat for every trainee adds up
categories.title: Licence & Environment Cost

questions.question: Your team wants to move from annotated screenshots to a full sandbox. What should they expect?

categories.analogy: A cookbook with photos: great for following along, but reading it doesn't make you able to cook.
categories.description: Annotated screenshot or video guides are the cheapest to create but are passive: learners watch and never practise.
categories.details: Someone with access does the task once, captures the screens or records a video, and adds numbered callouts or narration. It can be made in an afternoon and works for any software, web or desktop. But the learner only watches. Nothing checks whether they could do the task themselves, and every screenshot is a copy of pixels that goes out of date when the screen changes.
inScope: Step-by-step screenshot guides with callouts
Narrated screen recordings
Quick reference cards and job aids
outOfScope: Any practice where the learner clicks or types
categories.primaryFocus: Lowest build cost, any platform
categories.subtitle: Show, don't touch
categories.title: Annotated Screenshot & Video Guides

categories.analogy: A pop-up book: parts move when you pull the right tab, but you can't redraw a page without printing a new book.
categories.description: Screen-capture hotspot simulations turn recorded screens into clickable steps, but every UI change means re-recording the affected screens.
categories.details: An authoring tool records the real software as an expert performs the task, then turns each captured screen into a slide with an invisible 'hotspot' on the right button or field. The learner must click the right spot or type the right value to advance, and can get hints or feedback on wrong clicks. It works for desktop and web software alike. The catch: each slide is still a picture, so when a button moves in the next release, those screens have to be recorded again.
inScope: Click and type steps on captured screens
Hints and feedback for wrong clicks
Desktop and web applications
outOfScope: Free exploration off the recorded path
categories.primaryFocus: Real practice for any software, built by instructional designers
categories.subtitle: Recorded screens with clickable spots
categories.title: Hotspot Simulations

categories.analogy: Saving the recipe card instead of a photo of the cake: you can still change the ingredients afterwards.
categories.description: HTML/DOM capture demos snapshot real web pages so text and data can be edited without re-recording, but only work for web apps.
categories.details: Instead of a screenshot, a browser extension saves the page's HTML and CSS: the actual structure a browser renders. The result looks pixel-perfect and stays crisp at any screen size. Because it is still HTML, an author can change a customer name, a number or a label in an editor without capturing the screen again. Desktop software has no DOM to capture, so this only works for web apps, and a real layout change still means a new capture.
inScope: Browser-based SaaS and internal web apps
Editing text and fake data after capture
Guided and self-explore product demos
outOfScope: Desktop applications and terminals
Real server logic behind the captured pages
categories.primaryFocus: High visual realism for web apps with easy text edits
categories.subtitle: A snapshot of the real web page, not a picture of it
categories.title: HTML/DOM Capture Demos

categories.analogy: A film-set street built with real doors and windows: everything you touch works, but nobody lives there.
categories.description: A rebuilt UI clone with a mocked backend reuses the product's real front-end components, giving high fidelity and automated tests, but needs developers to maintain it.
categories.details: Developers assemble the training screens from the same component library the product uses, and replace the real server with a mock that returns prepared fake data. Buttons, forms and validation behave like the real thing, and learners can explore freely. Because it is code, it can be tested automatically and updated in the same pull request as the product. The price is that someone who can write front-end code has to own it.
inScope: Reusing the product's own UI components
Mock API responses with synthetic data
Automated tests for the training flow
outOfScope: Real back-end rules, integrations and batch jobs
categories.primaryFocus: Highest fidelity without a real backend
categories.subtitle: The real front end, a fake server
categories.title: UI Clone with a Mocked Backend

categories.analogy: A practice kitchen in a cooking school: real stoves and knives, but nobody is eating the food.
categories.description: A training sandbox is a separate real instance loaded with synthetic data; it is the most realistic but needs infrastructure, resets and its own access control.
categories.details: The organisation runs another copy of the real system just for training, filled with synthetic customers, orders or tickets. Everything the learner does is real software behaviour, including workflows, integrations with other sandboxes and error messages. But it must be hosted, kept on the same version as production, reset after each class so the next group starts clean, and given its own training accounts and roles.
inScope: Separate non-production instance of the real system
Synthetic data and scheduled resets
Training-only accounts and roles
outOfScope: Anything that touches production data or real customers
categories.primaryFocus: Maximum realism, including back-end behaviour
categories.subtitle: The real software, fake world
categories.title: Training Sandbox

categories.analogy: A photographer who follows you around and captions every photo.
categories.description: Scribe, Tango and Guidde auto-generate step-by-step screenshot guides from a recorded session; Snagit and Loom cover manual screenshots and video.
categories.details: With Scribe, Tango or Guidde you press record, do the task once, and the tool captures a screenshot and a written instruction for every click, then lets you blur sensitive data and share or export the guide. Snagit is the classic tool for hand-made annotated screenshots, and Loom records quick narrated screen videos.
inScope: Auto-captured step guides: Scribe, Tango, Guidde
Manual annotated screenshots: Snagit
Narrated screen videos: Loom
outOfScope: Clickable practice with feedback
categories.primaryFocus: Fastest path from doing a task to a shareable guide
categories.subtitle: Scribe · Tango · Guidde · Snagit · Loom
categories.title: Screenshot & Video Guide Tools

categories.analogy: A lesson-in-a-box that plugs into the school's register.
categories.description: Articulate Storyline 360, Adobe Captivate and iSpring Suite build hotspot simulations and publish them as SCORM or xAPI packages for an LMS.
categories.details: These e-learning authoring tools record the screen as an expert does the task and build clickable steps from it, with hints, feedback and scoring. They publish the result as a SCORM or xAPI package, a standard format that a learning management system (LMS) can host and use to record who finished the course and how they scored.
inScope: Screen recording into clickable steps
Hints, feedback and scoring
SCORM / xAPI packages for an LMS
outOfScope: Editing text without the authoring tool
categories.primaryFocus: Tracked, scored practice inside an LMS
categories.subtitle: Articulate Storyline 360 · Adobe Captivate · iSpring Suite
categories.title: Hotspot Simulation Authoring Tools

categories.analogy: A cardboard cut-out of the shop that still has working doors.
categories.description: Walnut, Navattic, Storylane and Reprise capture a web app's HTML/DOM into editable, clickable demos.
categories.details: These platforms use a browser extension to capture the pages of a web app, then let you edit text and data, add guided steps and share the demo as a link or an embed. They are often sold for product-marketing demos, but the same capture works for internal training on web systems.
inScope: Browser-extension capture of web pages
Editing text and data in a web editor
Sharing demos as a link or embed
outOfScope: Desktop software
categories.primaryFocus: Realistic web-app demos without the real backend
categories.subtitle: Walnut · Navattic · Storylane · Reprise
categories.title: HTML/DOM Capture Platforms

categories.analogy: Real Lego bricks from the product's own box, a pretend power supply, and a tour guide pointing at each brick.
categories.description: A UI clone is typically built with the product's component library in Storybook, Mock Service Worker (MSW) for the fake API, and a tour library such as Shepherd.js or Driver.js for guided steps.
categories.details: Storybook shows the product's real components in isolation and is a natural place to assemble training screens. Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts the app's network requests in the browser and answers them with fake data, so no real server is needed. Shepherd.js or Driver.js add the guided layer: highlight an element, explain it, and wait for the learner to act.
inScope: Storybook for the product's components
MSW for the fake API
Shepherd.js / Driver.js for guided steps
outOfScope: Authoring without developers
categories.primaryFocus: Building training screens from the product's own code
categories.subtitle: Storybook · Mock Service Worker (MSW) · Shepherd.js · Driver.js
categories.title: UI Clone Building Blocks

categories.analogy: A smoke alarm for your manual: it goes off the moment the real UI stops matching.
categories.description: Playwright tests plus visual-regression services such as Chromatic or Percy detect when the real UI has changed.
categories.details: Playwright drives a browser through the documented steps and fails if a button or field can no longer be found. Chromatic and Percy take screenshots of each screen on every build and highlight pixel differences against an approved baseline. Together they tell you which manual screens a release has broken, before learners find out.
inScope: Scripted checks that documented steps still work
Visual diffs against approved screenshots
outOfScope: Fixing the manual (they only tell you what broke)
categories.primaryFocus: Knowing when the manual is out of date
categories.subtitle: Playwright · Chromatic · Percy
categories.title: Drift Detection Tools

categories.analogy: A stage set you can build, strike and rebuild every night, with actors instead of real customers.
categories.description: Training sandboxes use vendor sandboxes (Salesforce sandboxes, ServiceNow sub-production instances) or Docker Compose/Terraform environments seeded by synthetic-data tools such as Faker, Mockaroo or Tonic.ai.
categories.details: Many SaaS vendors offer sandboxes out of the box, such as Salesforce sandboxes or ServiceNow sub-production instances. For self-hosted systems, Docker Compose or Terraform describe the environment so it can be created and reset the same way every time. Faker (a code library), Mockaroo (a web tool) and Tonic.ai (a data platform) produce realistic fake records to fill it.
inScope: Vendor sandboxes and sub-production instances
Environment definitions: Docker Compose, Terraform
Synthetic data: Faker, Mockaroo, Tonic.ai
outOfScope: Copies of production data
categories.primaryFocus: Repeatable environments with privacy-safe data
categories.subtitle: Salesforce sandboxes · ServiceNow sub-prod · Docker Compose · Terraform · Faker · Mockaroo · Tonic.ai
categories.title: Sandbox & Synthetic Data Tools

categories.description: UI clones and training sandboxes are naturally 'as code': components, MSW handlers, tour steps, Terraform and seed scripts live in git, get reviewed in pull requests and run in CI.
categories.details: A UI clone is front-end code: components, MSW handlers that fake the API, and tour steps for Shepherd.js or Driver.js. A sandbox is infrastructure code: Terraform or Docker Compose files plus seed scripts that fill it with synthetic data. Because everything is text in git, a change is a pull request that someone reviews, CI tests it, and a new version can be rebuilt the same way every time.

categories.description: Screenshot guides can become code by scripting Playwright to drive a non-production instance and capture every screenshot, so the whole manual regenerates on each release.
categories.details: Instead of a person clicking and capturing, a Playwright script logs into a staging or sandbox instance, performs each documented step and saves a screenshot. The text lives in Markdown next to it. On each release CI runs the script again, so every screenshot is fresh. If a step fails, the script tells you the manual needs a text change too. You do need a non-production instance for the script to run against.

categories.details: Storyline, Captivate and iSpring save projects as their own file formats that you edit in the desktop tool. Walnut, Navattic, Storylane and Reprise keep the demo inside their web platform. You can't easily see what changed between two versions, review it in a pull request, or rebuild it from a script. categories.description: AI is best used for drafting: step text and voice-over from recordings, quiz questions, synthetic data, and code changes to mocks and tour steps.
categories.details: Screenshot tools such as Scribe, Tango and Guidde already use AI to write step text and voice-over from a recording. A language model can draft quiz questions from the step script, generate realistic synthetic records, and, for as-code approaches, a coding assistant can propose the change to MSW handlers or tour steps after a UI release. In every case AI produces a first draft that is faster to review than to write.

categories.analogy: A sat-nav that invents a road: it only helps if someone checks the map before the trip.
categories.description: AI output must be verified against the real UI, by a person or by automated tests, because an invented step is exactly the drift a simulation must avoid.
categories.details: A language model can describe a button that isn't there or a menu path that the product never had, and say it confidently. To a learner that's the same failure as a stale screenshot: they rehearse something that doesn't exist. So AI drafts pass the same gate as human work: a person who knows the real UI checks it, or a Playwright test proves every step can actually be performed.

terms.detailedDefinition: A security principle under which accounts get the smallest set of roles necessary. It is why trainees often can't perform the very actions a manual must teach.
terms.shortDefinition: Giving each person only the permissions their current job needs.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the most common reason learners can't practise in the real system.

terms.detailedDefinition: The fidelity ladder runs from annotated screenshots to click-through walkthroughs, interactive simulations with fake data and a full sandbox. Higher fidelity gives more realistic practice at higher build and upkeep cost.
terms.shortDefinition: How closely a simulation matches the real software.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right rung is the first trade-off of any interactive manual.

terms.detailedDefinition: Controls, labels and order on the path the learner practises match the real software exactly; areas off the path can be static or disabled.
terms.shortDefinition: Exact on the task path, simplified everywhere else.
terms.whyItMatters: It keeps practice realistic where it counts while keeping cost down.

terms.detailedDefinition: In hotspot simulations, an invisible click target sits on the correct button or field of a captured screen. Clicking it advances the step; clicking elsewhere can trigger feedback.
terms.shortDefinition: A clickable area placed over a recorded screen.
terms.whyItMatters: Hotspots make recorded screens practisable, but the screens under them go stale with every UI change.

terms.detailedDefinition: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the structure a browser renders. Capturing it gives a crisp, realistic copy whose text and data can be edited without re-recording.
terms.shortDefinition: Saving a web page's HTML structure instead of a picture of it.
terms.whyItMatters: It's why DOM-capture demos are easier to update than screenshots, but only for web apps.

terms.detailedDefinition: MSW intercepts requests in the browser and returns prepared responses, so a UI clone runs with no real server.
terms.shortDefinition: A library that answers an app's network requests with fake data.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the fake backend of a UI clone.

terms.detailedDefinition: Authoring tools such as Storyline, Captivate and iSpring publish SCORM or xAPI packages. The LMS uses them to track completion and scores; xAPI can also record detailed events such as wrong clicks.
terms.shortDefinition: Standard formats that let an LMS host a course and record results.
terms.whyItMatters: It's how you measure who finished training and where they struggled.

terms.detailedDefinition: Fake customers, tickets or orders created with tools such as Faker, Mockaroo or Tonic.ai and shared as fixtures across simulations.
terms.shortDefinition: Invented records that look real but belong to nobody.

terms.detailedDefinition: Every release can move buttons, rename labels or change steps. Unless someone updates the simulation, learners rehearse screens that no longer exist.
terms.shortDefinition: When the manual no longer matches the real software.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the central failure mode of interactive manuals: the Drifted Phantom UI.

terms.detailedDefinition: Services such as Chromatic and Percy capture screens on every build and highlight pixel differences against a baseline.
terms.shortDefinition: Comparing new screenshots with approved ones to spot changes.
terms.whyItMatters: It tells you which manual screens a release has changed.

terms.detailedDefinition: UI clones, sandbox definitions and scripted screenshot guides live in git, so changes are pull requests, tests run automatically and everything can be rebuilt.
terms.shortDefinition: Keeping the manual as text files in git, reviewed and built by CI.
terms.whyItMatters: It makes upkeep reviewable, testable and repeatable.

terms.detailedDefinition: The three simulation modes: Watch shows the task, Try lets the learner do it with hints and feedback, and Test checks they can do it alone.
terms.shortDefinition: Demo, guided practice with hints, then unguided assessment.
terms.whyItMatters: It moves learners from seeing to doing to proving.

categories.analogy: A phrasebook organised by situations ('at the restaurant', 'at the station') beats a dictionary when you're travelling.
categories.description: Organise the manual around real job tasks (e.g. 'approve a leave request'), not a tour of every screen and menu.
categories.details: Learners come to a manual to get a job done. A tour of every menu ('this is the File menu, this is the Settings tab…') is easy to write because it follows the software, but people forget it immediately because it isn't attached to anything they need to do. Start from the list of tasks each role performs and build one module per task.
inScope: A task list per role
One module per job task
outOfScope: Feature tours of every menu
categories.primaryFocus: Modules that map to real work
categories.subtitle: Teach jobs, not menus
categories.title: Task-First, Not Screen-First

categories.analogy: A film set only builds the side of the street the camera sees.
categories.description: Selective fidelity: copy the controls, labels and order on the task path exactly; everything off the path can be static or disabled.
categories.details: The learner's muscle memory is built on the path they practise, so the buttons, labels, field order and messages on that path must match the real software exactly. Everything else on the screen (other menus, side panels, unrelated tabs) can be a static picture or a disabled control. This keeps build and upkeep cost down without making practice less real where it counts.
inScope: Exact labels, controls and order on the task path
Static or disabled areas off the path
outOfScope: Rebuilding every feature of the product
categories.primaryFocus: Realism where it matters, low cost elsewhere
categories.subtitle: Exact on the path, simple off it
categories.title: Selective Fidelity

categories.analogy: A good crash-test dummy is shaped like a person, but it isn't one.
categories.description: Use synthetic data that looks like real cases, never copied production data.
categories.details: 'Test User 1' and 'Lorem ipsum' make practice feel fake and hide the real difficulty, such as long names, duplicate customers or an order with ten line items. Invent synthetic records that look like the cases learners will meet, including the awkward ones. Never copy production data into a training tool, even 'just for now'.
inScope: Synthetic records modelled on real cases
Edge cases learners will meet
outOfScope: Copies of production data
categories.primaryFocus: Practice that feels real without privacy risk
categories.subtitle: Believable cases, zero real people
categories.title: Realistic, Safe Data

categories.analogy: A flight simulator lets you crash, shows you why, and puts you back on the runway.
categories.description: Make it safe to fail: learners can make mistakes, see what would happen, and reset.
categories.details: The whole point of simulating is that errors cost nothing, so use it. Let learners press the wrong button and show them what would happen in the real system ('This would have refunded the customer twice'). Then give them a one-click reset so they can try again from a clean start.
inScope: Showing the consequence of a wrong action
One-click reset to a clean start
outOfScope: Silently blocking every wrong click
categories.primaryFocus: Learning from consequences without real damage
categories.subtitle: Mistakes are the lesson
categories.title: Safe to Fail

categories.analogy: Recipe cards instead of a cookbook read cover to cover.
categories.description: Keep each module to one short task with one goal, so learners can finish it in a few minutes and look it up again later.
categories.details: A 45-minute simulation of 'everything in the CRM' is hard to finish and impossible to find again when you need it. A module called 'Merge two duplicate customers' takes three minutes and can be found by searching for the task on the day you need it. Short modules are also easier to update: a release breaks one small module, not a giant course.
inScope: One goal per module
Task names learners would search for
outOfScope: Long all-in-one courses
categories.primaryFocus: Finishable and findable modules
categories.subtitle: One task, one goal, a few minutes
categories.title: Small Chunks

categories.analogy: The driving instructor's last lesson: 'on the motorway, nobody will brake for you'.
categories.description: End each task with a bridge to the real system: what differs there, such as extra approvals, permissions or live consequences.
categories.details: A simulation always leaves something out. Close each module by telling learners what will be different when they do it for real: 'In the live system your manager must approve refunds over 5,000 baht', 'You will only see this menu after your role is granted', 'This e-mail really goes to the customer'. It stops practice-world habits from causing real-world surprises.
inScope: Extra approvals and permissions in the real system
Consequences that are live for real
outOfScope: Pretending the simulation is identical
categories.primaryFocus: Transferring practice safely to the live system
categories.subtitle: Say what's different out there
categories.title: Bridge to the Real System

categories.analogy: A building's ramp isn't an extra; it's how some people get in the door.
categories.description: Make the simulation accessible: keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels and captions for any audio or video.
categories.details: If some staff use the real system with a keyboard or a screen reader, the manual must work that way too. Hotspots that only respond to a mouse click lock them out. Give every control a keyboard path and a screen-reader label, and caption every narration or video.
inScope: Keyboard navigation
Screen-reader labels
Captions for audio and video
outOfScope: Mouse-only hotspots
categories.primaryFocus: Nobody is left out of training
categories.subtitle: Everyone who uses the system can train on it
categories.title: Accessible
